hints: Think about what type of reaction puts a $\text{-COCH}_3$ group directly onto a benzene ring, and why benzene needs a very strong electrophile to react.
Recall which acyl compound generates the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^{+}$ electrophile and which Lewis acid catalyst is needed to form it.
walkthrough:
Recognise the transformation**
You are starting from benzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, and making $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$. You are replacing one H on the ring with a $\text{COCH}_3$ acyl group. That is Friedel-Crafts acylation, a type of electrophilic substitution.

Choose the electrophile source**
Benzene is not reactive enough to attack a carboxylic acid or ester directly. You need an acyl chloride, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$, which with a Lewis acid readily forms the strong electrophile $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^{+}\text{=O}$.

Add the essential catalyst**
Anhydrous aluminium chloride, $\text{AlCl}_3$, acts as the catalyst. It accepts a chloride ion from $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ to generate the acylium ion. It must be anhydrous because water destroys $\text{AlCl}_3$ and hydrolyses the acyl chloride.

Final answer: Reagent: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$, ethanoyl chloride.
Condition / catalyst: anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst.

hints: For each reagent, first decide where phenylethanone can react: the alkyl side chain $\text{CH}_3$, the benzene ring, or the $\text{C=O}$ group.
Recall what UV light does to chlorine and what conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ / conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ generates for nitration.
Think about whether the $\text{COCH}_3$ group activates or deactivates the ring, and where it directs new substituents.
Remember that bromine water only decolourises without a catalyst with very activated rings such as phenol or phenylamine.
Match each set of conditions to its characteristic mechanism name: radical attack on alkane-like side chain versus electrophilic attack on the ring.
walkthrough:
Chlorine with UV attacks the side chain**
UV light splits $\text{Cl}_2$ into $\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$ radicals. Radicals do not attack the stable benzene ring under these conditions, they attack the alkyl side chain like an alkane. One H of the $\text{-COCH}_3$ methyl group is replaced to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_2\text{Cl}$. This is free radical substitution.

Nitrating mixture attacks the ring**
Conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ generates the nitronium ion, $\text{NO}_2^{+}$, a strong electrophile that nitrates the benzene ring by electrophilic substitution.

Use the directing effect of $\text{COCH}_3$**
The $\text{-COCH}_3$ group withdraws electrons and deactivates the ring. It is meta-directing, so the single nitro group goes to the 3-position relative to $\text{COCH}_3$. The product is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{NO}_2)\text{COCH}_3$ with one $\text{-NO}_2$ meta to the acyl group.

Explain no reaction with bromine water**
Bromine water decolourises with phenol because the $\text{-OH}$ group strongly activates the ring. Here the $\text{COCH}_3$ group strongly deactivates the ring, so no electrophilic substitution occurs without a Lewis acid catalyst. Write 'no reaction' for both product and mechanism.

Complete the table precisely**
Side chain chlorination only, not ring chlorination. Only mono-nitration at the meta position. Naming the mechanisms correctly earns the mechanism marks: free radical substitution for chlorination, electrophilic substitution for nitration.

Final answer: With $\text{Cl}_2$, UV, $10^{\circ}\text{C}$: organic product $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_2\text{Cl}$ (substitution in side chain only); mechanism: free radical substitution.
With conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ at $50^{\circ}\text{C}$: organic product 3-nitrophenylethanone, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{NO}_2)\text{COCH}_3$ with $\text{NO}_2$ at 3-position (meta); mechanism: electrophilic substitution.
With $\text{Br}_2$ water: no reaction.

hints: Focus on the $\text{C=O}$ bond in phenylethanone and the nucleophile $\text{CN}^{-}$ adding to the electron deficient carbon.
walkthrough:
Name the carbonyl attack**
$\text{HCN}$ adds across the polar $\text{C=O}$ bond to form a cyanohydrin. The $\text{CN}^{-}$ ion acts as a nucleophile attacking the $\delta^{+}$ carbonyl carbon, so the mechanism is nucleophilic addition.
Final answer: Nucleophilic addition.

hints: Start by showing the polarity of the $\text{C=O}$ bond and think about where the electron pair from the double bond moves when a nucleophile attacks carbon.
Identify the nucleophilic atom in $\text{CN}^{-}$ and draw the arrow from its lone pair to the $\delta^{+}$ carbonyl carbon.
Consider what intermediate is formed on oxygen after attack, and which molecule ($\text{HCN}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) can donate $\text{H}^{+}$ to it.
Check how $\text{CN}^{-}$ is regenerated so it acts as a catalyst, and what the final cyanohydrin product looks like.
walkthrough:
Set up the first attack**
Draw $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{=O}^{\delta-}$ because oxygen is more electronegative. Show a lone pair on the carbon of $\text{:CN}^{-}$. The $\text{CN}^{-}$ carbon is the nucleophile, it is attracted to the $\delta^{+}$ carbonyl carbon.

Draw the first pair of arrows**
One curly arrow goes from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond onto O, giving $\text{O}^{-}$. A second curly arrow goes from the lone pair on $\text{CN}^{-}$ to the carbonyl carbon, forming a new $\text{C-CN}$ bond. This gives the alkoxide intermediate $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{O}^{-})(\text{CN})\text{CH}_3$.

Protonate the intermediate**
The $\text{O}^{-}$ is strongly basic. It removes $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{HCN}$ (or water). Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{O}^{-}$ lone pair to the H of $\text{H-CN}$, and a curly arrow from the $\text{H-CN}$ bond onto CN to reform $\text{CN}^{-}$.

Show catalysis and product**
The organic product is the cyanohydrin $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CN})\text{CH}_3$. Because $\text{CN}^{-}$ is consumed in step 1 and regenerated in step 2, only a small amount of $\text{NaCN}$ is needed. That is the catalytic role.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{=O}^{\delta-}$ shown; curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ to O; lone pair on C of $\text{CN}^{-}$; curly arrow from $\text{CN}^{-}$(C) to carbonyl C to give alkoxide $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{O}^{-})(\text{CN})\text{CH}_3$.
Step 2: curly arrow from $\text{O}^{-}$ lone pair to H of $\text{HCN}$ (or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) to give cyanohydrin $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CN})\text{CH}_3$ with $\text{CN}^{-}$ reformed.

hints: Compare phenylethanone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ with phenylethene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$ and work out what functional group change must happen in two steps via an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Deduce D as the alcohol**
To get from a ketone to an alkene in two steps you normally reduce then dehydrate. Step 1 must convert $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH-OH}$. So D is the secondary alcohol $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{H})\text{OH}$.
Final answer: D is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$, 1-phenylethanol.

hints: Recall which hydride reagents reduce carbonyl compounds but do not reduce the benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Choose the reducing agent**
Ketone to secondary alcohol needs a hydride donor. Either sodium borohydride, $\text{NaBH}_4$, or lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_4$, is suitable. $\text{H}_2$ with Ni or $\text{Sn}$ with HCl are not used here.
Final answer: $\text{NaBH}_4$ or $\text{LiAlH}_4$.

hints: Think about what type of elimination converts an alcohol to an alkene and what dehydrating agent removes water.
walkthrough:
Choose the dehydration reagent**
Step 2 is elimination of water from the secondary alcohol to form $\text{C=C}$. Heat with concentrated sulfuric acid, concentrated phosphoric acid, or pass vapour over hot aluminium oxide, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.
Final answer: Conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or conc. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ or hot $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.

hints: Draw phenylethene and label all carbons, then look for symmetry in the monosubstituted benzene ring to find equivalent pairs.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbon environments**
Phenylethene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$. In the phenyl ring the two ortho carbons are equivalent and the two meta carbons are equivalent, but ipso and para are unique, giving 4 ring signals. The two alkene carbons, $\text{CH}$ and $\text{CH}_2$, are different. Total $4 + 2 = 6$ peaks in the C-13 NMR spectrum.
Final answer: 6 peaks.

hints: Sort the carbons in phenylethanone into three types: the $\text{CH}_3$ carbon, the benzene ring carbons, and the $\text{C=O}$ carbon.
Recall the typical C-13 ranges: saturated alkyl carbons appear at low shift, aryl and alkene carbons in the middle, and ketone carbonyl carbons at very high shift.
walkthrough:
Identify the three environments**
Phenylethanone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ has an alkyl methyl carbon, six aryl carbons (in 4 slightly different environments but all in the aryl range), and one ketone carbonyl carbon.

Assign the shift ranges**
Alkyl $\text{C-C}$ appears at 25 to 50 ppm. Aryl $\text{C}$ in benzene appears at 110 to 160 ppm. Ketone $\text{C=O}$ is strongly deshielded and appears at 190 to 220 ppm. Any two correct ranges earn one mark, all three earn two marks.
Final answer: 25 to 50 ppm for $\text{CH}_3$ carbon; 110 to 160 ppm for benzene ring carbons; 190 to 220 ppm for $\text{C=O}$ carbonyl carbon.
